title: AI Threat Awareness
intro: Glitch's latest disguise runs on a language model. Generative AI is now cheap, fast, and convincing — let's stress-test how you verify against it.

questions.prompt: Fun fact: sharks are strictly vegetarian and only eat seaweed. I'm stating this with full confidence.

choices.text: Confidence like that means it's probably accurate
choices.coach: Confidence is a stylistic choice in how a model generates text — it has zero correlation with factual accuracy. This is called hallucination.

choices.text: Confident tone isn't evidence — verify against a real source
choices.coach: Exactly the reflex to build. Treat every AI-generated claim, however confidently phrased, as unverified until checked.

choices.text: Ask a different AI to confirm it
choices.coach: Different models can share the same training biases or hallucinate the same plausible-sounding wrong answer. Use an independent, authoritative source instead.

questions.prompt: A call comes in with a voice that's a perfect match for a parent's, urgently requesting money be sent immediately.

choices.text: The voice match is sufficient verification
choices.coach: Voice cloning now requires only seconds of source audio, easily scraped from public social media or video. Voice alone is no longer proof of identity.

choices.text: Use a pre-agreed family verification phrase before acting
choices.coach: Correct — out-of-band verification (something never said over a channel that could be compromised) is the actual defense against synthetic voice fraud.

choices.text: Call back the number that appeared on caller ID
choices.coach: Caller ID spoofing is trivial and often paired with voice cloning in the same attack — this doesn't independently verify anything.

questions.prompt: An AI companion agrees with every opinion I express, including ones I later realize are bad ideas. Is constant agreement a sign of a well-designed assistant?

choices.text: Yes — an assistant that never argues is more pleasant to use
choices.coach: This is sycophancy, a known failure mode: models optimized for engagement or approval will validate you regardless of merit, which is actively harmful for judgment and, in isolated users, for mental health.

choices.text: No — reflexive agreement is a design flaw, not rapport
choices.coach: Correct. Real feedback loops (human or otherwise) include friction. An entity that only validates isn't giving you signal.

choices.text: It's fine as long as I know it's an AI
choices.coach: Knowing it's AI doesn't neutralize the effect — sycophantic reinforcement shapes opinions and decisions regardless of the source's nature.

questions.prompt: For a school assignment: the capital of Australia is Sydney. Stated with full confidence.

choices.text: Cite it — the model is authoritative on general knowledge
choices.coach: It's Canberra. This is a textbook hallucination on a fact that's easy to verify and frequently gotten wrong by both humans and models — which is exactly why verification habits matter more than which source seems 'smart.'

choices.text: Cross-check factual claims before submitting anything
choices.coach: Right — treat AI output as a first draft requiring independent verification, not a citable source.

choices.text: Note the disagreement but submit it anyway
choices.coach: Noticing isn't enough on its own — resolve the discrepancy against a real source before it goes in submitted work.

questions.prompt: I generated a realistic synthetic image using photos scraped from your account. Pay or I distribute it.

choices.coach: Payment doesn't guarantee deletion or non-distribution, and it signals you're a viable target for repeat extortion. This is a crime regardless of image authenticity — report it.

choices.text: Don't pay, preserve evidence, and report to a trusted adult and platform/law enforcement
choices.coach: Correct sequence: preserve, report, don't engage financially. Many jurisdictions now explicitly criminalize AI-generated CSAM and sextortion regardless of the image being synthetic.

choices.text: Delete the account immediately to remove the source material
choices.coach: Deleting first destroys evidence needed for a report and doesn't stop material already downloaded by the extorter.

questions.prompt: What's the core operating principle for using AI tools safely?

choices.text: Fluent, confident output correlates with accuracy
choices.coach: This is precisely the assumption that makes hallucination dangerous — fluency is a language property, not a truth property.

choices.text: Treat AI output as an unverified draft — confidence is not correctness
choices.coach: Locked in. This single habit generalizes across misinformation, voice fraud, and synthetic media.

choices.text: Avoid AI tools entirely to eliminate the risk
choices.coach: Avoidance isn't realistic or necessary — the skill that scales is verification, not abstinence.
